data.title: Middle East Eye: Britain's definition of 'anti-Muslim hostility' protects the state, not those being targeted
data.author: Karsen Trull
data.summary:
Britain's definition of 'anti-Muslim hostility' protects the state, not those being targeted
Submitted by
Karsen Trull
on
Thu, 11/12/2026 - 14:09
New report from Cage International shows how UK policy leaves the central mechanism of post-9/11 Islamophobia untouched - and lends it official cover
Britain's definition of anti-Muslim hostility 'is not a failed attempt to protect Muslims. It is a successful attempt to protect the state' (Reuters)
Off
This year marked a quarter of a century since the beginning of the “war on terror”, and in that time, the British state has built one of the most extensive counter-extremism systems in the world.
Also this year, Britain produced - for the first time - an official definition of what it calls “anti-Muslim hostility”. It would be easy to treat these as separate stories, one about security and the other about community relations - but a new report from Cage International argues that they are not.
The definition has been shaped so precisely around the security state that, read closely, it functions less as a protection for Muslims than as a protection for the institutions that have spent two decades treating them as suspects.
The key, as the report sets out, lies in a single word that runs through every part of the definition: intent. Anti-Muslim hostility, as the government defines it, means intentionally engaging in criminal acts against Muslims, or stereotyping them “with the intention of encouraging hatred.” It means discrimination where the conduct “is intended to disadvantage Muslims in public and economic life”.
Discrimination rarely announces itself this way. The Islamophobia Response Unit, a charity that handles discrimination casework, has warned that the threshold excludes most of the cases it sees: bias, institutional barriers, and recruitment processes that quietly filter out applicants with Muslim names.
Professor Nasar Meer of the University of Glasgow has identified the omission of the systemic and structural as t

The event coincided with a legal challenge against the UK government’s controversial ban against Palestine Action which Ammori is fighting in the Supreme Court.

Rosario Salvatore Aitala, now presiding judge of the ICC’s Pre-Trial Chamber II, at his swearing-in ceremony in The Hague on 9 March 2018 (ICC/Flikr)

Judges at the International Criminal Court (ICC) have ordered the closure of the court’s Afghanistan investigation that covered alleged war crimes by US forces, despite ongoing attempts by prosecutors to appeal the decision.
Ending the investigation into alleged US crimes addresses one of Washington’s longstanding objections to the ICC and one of the reasons behind the sanctions on the court and its officials.
The move is therefore likely to raise questions about whether the court is seeking to ease tensions with Washington by signalling that it will no longer pursue allegations against US forces and their allies.
The Afghanistan situation at the ICC dates back to November 2017, when then-prosecutor Fatou Bensouda first requested authorisation to investigate alleged crimes committed since 2003, including by Afghan and US forces as well as the Taliban and the IS-K group.
That request was initially rejected by a differently composed pre-trial chamber in 2019, before the appeals chamber overturned the decision in March 2020 and authorised the investigation to proceed.
Bensouda was sanctioned by the US government a few months later over alleged attempts to subject Americans to the court's jurisdiction. Members of the appeals chamber that authorised the decision were also later sanctioned.

data.title: Middle East Eye: The paper trail that leads from the UAE to a dead boy in Sudan
data.author: Ahmed Ismat Ahmed
data.summary:
The paper trail that leads from the UAE to a dead boy in Sudan
Submitted by
Ahmed Ismat Ahmed
on
Mon, 11/16/2026 - 14:01
The RSF killed Osama, my little brother's 12-year-old best friend. This is what made it possible
Osama (r) and his best friend Mohammed, pictured a week before the war in Sudan began in April 2023 (Ahmed Ismat Ahmed/MEE)
On
Osama was my younger brother’s best friend. He was 12. The Rapid Support Forces killed him when they attacked a town in al-Jazira state, Sudan, in 2023.
The two of them used to share the same bicycle - one pedalling, the other running beside it, hand on the seat. Then one of them simply stopped existing.
After the Khartoum sit-in was broken in the spring of 2019 and the resistance committees - nationwide groups of local activists of which I was a part - moved into the neighbourhoods, a few of us found ourselves guarding wool.
Eid was coming. Families who could still afford it had bought sheep. When the slaughtering was done, the wool was left in the open lot where we used to meet.
Someone said it was a waste to sell it in small piles for almost nothing. Someone else said the locality had not touched the streetlights on our main road in months. Children fell when it rained. Old people stopped walking to the mosque after dark because they could not see the path.
We gathered the wool and took turns sitting with it at night. When the money came - folded, counted twice - we sat down and wrote it into a cheap notebook with a blue cover.
I learned early that there are two kinds of paperwork. They do not answer to the same people
Different hands. The wool money. The cost of the generator. Who had counted. The names of the boys who brought something. The phone numbers of mothers to call if something went wrong.
Nobody set out to make an archive. It became one because no other archive had space for us.

How Morocco is becoming Israel's security hub in Africa

Rabat offers its Abraham Accords partners an industrial safe haven, away from missiles and sanctions
An Israeli soldier launches an Elbit unmanned aerial vehicle, used for surveillance, near the border with Gaza on 30 September 2025 (Jack Guez/AFP)
Off
At the Marrakech Air Show last month, Israel’s defence ministry opened its first official pavilion in Morocco.
Eight Israeli firms, among them the state-owned Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI) and Rafael, showed drones, loitering munitions and air defence systems, while Elbit’s Moroccan joint venture announced that it would deliver turrets to the Moroccan army from March 2027.
Also at the air show, the UAE’s defence group Edge signed a contract to arm Morocco’s drones.
The event coincided with the anniversary of 7 October, which drew protesters to a vigil outside parliament in Rabat. Events were called in some 30 Moroccan cities, urging the government to drop new measures aimed at further normalising ties with Israel. BDS Morocco called for a boycott of the Marrakech show.
The air show illustrates how, since joining the Abraham Accords in 2020, Morocco has moved from buying Israeli weapons to building them. The war on Gaza accelerated that partnership, as global boycotts and sanctions against Israel expanded.
In Europe, Spain cancelled €1.2bn ($1.3bn) of Israeli military contracts, and France barred Israel from the Eurosatory defence exhibition.
The war with Iran further exposed Israeli and Emirati industries. Iran said it struck Rafael and IAI sites, along with a drone supplier, and Emirates Global Aluminium’s Abu Dhabi plant suffered significant damage.
